title: A Road of Our Own
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 29 of 40
content:
The road outside Ba Sing Se smelled of wet earth and somebody else's breakfast.

I had expected leaving the city to feel like a grand beginning. Instead my pack strap rubbed my shoulder, one cart wheel squealed behind us, and Iroh stopped at the first crossroads to argue with a stubborn kettle.

"It is not arguing," he told me when I pointed this out. "It is expressing uncertainty about the lid."

"The kettle?"

"Naturally."

He turned the lid twice, found the small bend in the rim, and settled it with his thumb. The steam stopped escaping from one side.

"There," he said. "We have achieved peace."

"We've gone less than a mile."

"A promising start."

The journey was supposed to be ours.

No diplomatic visit, no errand for the teahouse, no obligation to make an appearance as the Dragon of the West. I had chosen a little market town beside the river and an inn that advertised clean beds rather than important guests. Iroh had selected the scenic route, though I suspected he had also chosen it because the road passed a tea stall he remembered from years ago.

We had agreed to tell one another when we wanted something instead of leaving the other to perform the guessing.

It sounded simple until we actually tried.

At a fork where the dirt road split around a ridge, Iroh pointed left.

"The river route will be pleasant in this weather."

"The innkeeper's map says the footbridge has been repaired only halfway."

"An inconvenience we can assess when we arrive."

I looked at the cloud bank gathering above the hills.

"I'd rather not assess a broken bridge in the rain."

He smiled his gentle, infuriating smile.

"Prudence is admirable."

"Then let's practice it."

He looked surprised enough that I laughed.

"I'm serious. I want the upper road."

He studied the map, then folded it carefully.

"Then we shall take the upper road."

"You don't mind?"

"Of course I mind a little. I wanted to show you the river. But I asked what you wanted, and you answered."

We walked for a while in companionable silence. The upper road wound past terraced fields where a group of farmers was repairing a washout. A woman in a straw hat called for the next basket of stones, and two younger workers passed it along without looking up. Iroh slowed, watching the work.

"Do you want to help?" I asked.

"I want to know whether they need help. That is different."

He approached and asked. The woman said they had enough hands but could use dry rope from the next supply cart.

We had no rope.

He thanked her and returned to me.

"See?" I said.

"An excellent lesson in the limits of an elderly man's enthusiasm."

"You are not elderly when you want to climb hills."

"My knees disagree."

By midday the rain arrived. We took shelter beneath the roof of a roadside stall where the owner sold steamed buns and served tea in chipped cups. The owner, Mei, recognized Iroh almost immediately.

"General?"

I saw his shoulders stiffen.

For a heartbeat he looked as though he had been pulled into another year, one he hadn't asked to visit.

Then he inclined his head.

"These days, simply Iroh."

Mei looked at the kettle and the worn traveling bags.

"Oh. I'm sorry."

"Nothing to apologize for. Do you have something warm for two hungry travelers?"

She made us room.

Her buns were filled with greens and a sharp little pepper that made my eyes water. Iroh ate his slowly, praising the dough without telling her how to run her stall. When she went to help another customer, I leaned close.

"That was hard."

"Being recognized?"

"Not correcting her more sharply."

He turned the cup between his hands.

"I was once a general. She did not invent the title. I cannot ask people to forget what it meant simply because I have chosen a different life."

"You can still tell her what name you'd rather use."

"I did."

I touched the edge of his sleeve.

"Did you want me to say something?"

He considered.

"Not then. Thank you for noticing."

Across the stall, Mei argued with a supplier about the cost of charcoal. The seller wanted a higher price because the rain had ruined half the road. Mei protested that she couldn't raise the bun price without losing customers.

Iroh listened, then drew a small figure on his napkin.

"What are you doing?" I whispered.

"Calculating how many buns she must sell to pay for the better fuel."

"Are you going to give her a lecture?"

"No. I am trying to understand why she seems frightened."

When Mei returned, he asked whether she'd like help working through the figures. She said yes. He didn't suggest magic or a rich patron; he helped her separate the one-time transport cost from her normal weekly expense. She thanked him, and he paid for our meal at the full posted price.

Outside, the rain thinned.

"We didn't fix the whole world," I said.

"No."

"Good."

He laughed.

We reached the inn before dusk. The woman at the desk had one room overlooking the lane and a second, smaller one facing the garden. I asked to see them before deciding.

Iroh watched me with an expression somewhere between pride and amusement.

"What?" I asked.

"Nothing."

"I know that face."

"It is the face of a man pleased to travel with someone who knows what they want."

"I didn't always."

"Neither did I."

We chose the garden room. It was small enough that two people could not move around the bed without apologizing, and the shutters rattled whenever the wind changed. But it had a dry roof, clean water, and a view of the river through the branches.

I unpacked my notebook while Iroh warmed the kettle.

He set two cups on the sill.

"I had hoped to show you the river at sunset," he said.

"You did. We can see it from here."

"Not from the bridge."

"The bridge would have been a terrible date."

He looked offended.

"It might have been a memorable one."

"Memorably wet."

He chuckled.

I watched him pour tea, then asked the question that had followed me since the city.

"Is this difficult for you? Going somewhere without a purpose you can justify to everyone else?"

He sat down carefully.

"Yes."

I waited.

"I traveled for campaigns," he said. "Then for a boy I loved and feared for. There was always a reason bigger than my own wishes. An ordinary journey can leave too much room for the people who are no longer walking beside me."

I thought of Lu Ten and didn't ask him to make his grief easier for my benefit.

"I don't want this trip to replace anything," I said.

"I know."

"I love the life you've made. But I don't want to become another task you complete correctly."

Iroh looked at me over his cup.

"That would be a very poor arrangement for both of us."

I laughed softly.

He reached across the little table.

"May I?"

I put my hand in his. He turned it gently, waiting until I threaded our fingers together.

We had already spoken about my ethical non-monogamy and the fact that I preferred polyamory. He knew I had other relationships, other homes and obligations. This trip was not a demand that those roads disappear. It was the time we had each chosen to give.

"Would you like to see the town tomorrow?" he asked.

"Yes. But I want to choose the breakfast place."

"An alarming amount of power."

"I plan to abuse it."

He laughed so warmly I felt the sound settle in my chest.

When the rain grew heavier, we closed the shutters. The room smelled of tea and damp cedar. I sat beside him on the narrow bed and leaned into the warmth of his shoulder.

"Would you like a kiss?" he asked.

"Very much."

He kissed me without hurry, then rested his forehead against mine. We stayed there a while, listening to the river, until the candle burned low. The rest of the night was private.

In the morning, the road had dried enough for travel. The innkeeper warned that the lower footbridge remained closed. We thanked her for the information.

Iroh folded the map.

"Upper road?" he asked.

"Upper road."

He offered his arm.

I took it because I wanted to, and we went to find the breakfast place together.
